title: Why Does Your Leg KICK When You Tap Your Knee? 🦵
description:
Cross your legs and tap just under your kneecap. Did your foot kick on its own? That wasn't you: the tap stretches your thigh muscle a tiny bit, a stretch sensor in it pings your spinal cord, and the spinal cord fires the muscle straight back, all in about a fiftieth of a second (around 18 milliseconds), before your brain is even asked. No kick? Clench your teeth and tap again: doctors use the same kind of trick (the Jendrassik manoeuvre) to make the reflex bigger. And in 1902 Edwin Twitmyer, at the University of Pennsylvania, rang a bell just before every tap of his knee hammers; after about 150 rounds the bell alone made his volunteers' legs kick. He told the American Psychological Association in 1904 and nobody asked a single question. Pavlov's dogs got famous instead. Did your leg kick? Yes or no?
